lead: The heart makes about 1 mV at the skin. The ECG recording system picks this up with electrodes, amplifies it with a differential bio-amplifier, filters it, and draws it on a grid with fixed voltage and time scales. Every clinic, ICU, ambulance and home Holter uses this chain. Vectorcardiography draws the same activity as a loop in space, showing the heart's electrical axis more directly than twelve separate traces.
prereq: You need: resting and action potentials on cardiac potentials, electrode theory on electrode impedance, and bio-amplifiers and data acquisition on bio-amplifiers.

sections.h3: Twelve views of one signal: the standard leads

blocks.text: A lead is a view: a fixed pair of electrodes with defined polarity, so the same heart looks different from different angles. A bipolar lead measures voltage between two active electrodes. A unipolar lead measures one exploring electrode against a common reference built from the others.

The three standard limb leads use right arm (RA), left arm (LA) and left leg (LL). Lead I = LA − RA, II = LL − RA, III = LL − LA. Adding I and III gives LL − RA, which is lead II. This is Einthoven's law: II = I + III, a check on any limb-lead recording.
RA, LA and LL sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle with the heart at its centre, the Einthoven triangle. Each lead therefore looks along a fixed axis in the frontal plane.

The Wilson central terminal, WCT = (RA + LA + LL)/3, is the unipolar reference. The augmented limb leads leave the measured limb out of the reference: aVR = RA − (LA + LL)/2, which is 1.5 times RA − WCT, so the trace grows by half again, hence the letter a. The six chest leads V1–V6 are unipolar against WCT and look from the front and left side. Three bipolar limb leads, three augmented leads and six chest leads make the standard 12-lead ECG.

sections.h3: The recording chain and its two scales

blocks.text: The signal path is fixed: electrodes, lead selector, buffer, bio-amplifier, filters, ADC, display. The buffer has input impedance above 10 MΩ so electrode impedance does not divide down the signal. The bio-amplifier is differential, gain near 1000, common-mode rejection ratio above 100 dB to kill 50 Hz mains pickup. Filters remove baseline drift below 0.05 Hz and muscle noise above 150 Hz. A 12-bit ADC converts the trace for storage and display.

Two scales make the paper readable. Voltage: 1 mV = 10 mm at standard gain (10 mm/mV). Time: standard paper speed 25 mm/s, so 1 mm = 0.04 s and a large 5 mm square = 0.2 s. At 60 beats per minute the RR interval is 1 s = 25 mm.
time = length / speed   and   heart rate = 60 / RR
blocks.where: time is in s; length is the distance on paper in mm; speed is the paper speed in mm/s (25 or 50); RR is the interval between two QRS complexes in s; heart rate is in beats per minute. At 25 mm/s, heart rate = 1500 / (RR in mm).

items: Switch on, let it settle, press the 1 mV button and confirm the calibration bar is exactly 10 mm tall.
Select the lead, check the trace is free of 50 Hz fuzz, record.
Measure widths in mm, divide by paper speed to get seconds.
Measure heights in mm, divide by 10 to get mV.

blocks.text: The calibration pulse is the machine's honesty check. On maintenance rounds, wipe electrodes, inspect the patient cable for breaks, and confirm the bar is 10 mm on every channel.

sections.h3: Reading the waves, and the vector loop

blocks.text: The trace repeats in a fixed order: P wave (atrial depolarisation), PR segment, QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation), ST segment, T wave (ventricular repolarisation). Normal values at 25 mm/s are given below.

head: Feature
Normal duration
Normal amplitude
rows: 0.06–0.10 s normal; 0.10–0.12 s borderline; 0.12 s or more wide

items: Tall P above 0.25 mV suggests atrial enlargement.
PR longer than 0.20 s is first-degree AV block.
QRS of 0.12 s or more means slow conduction, as in bundle branch block, or a ventricular origin.
Raised ST suggests injury; sagging ST suggests ischaemia.
Flat or inverted T waves and tall peaked T waves are both abnormal.
No P waves with an irregularly irregular RR interval: atrial fibrillation.
Wide QRS complexes at 150–250 bpm with no P waves: ventricular tachycardia.
Raised ST, later deep Q waves, in the leads facing one wall of the heart: myocardial infarction.

blocks.text: Vectorcardiography (VCG) records the same dipole but keeps its direction. The Frank lead system uses seven electrodes (five around the chest, one on the back of the neck, one on the left leg), plus a ground electrode if used, to produce three orthogonal components X, Y and Z: X to the left (positive at the left), Y head to foot (positive at the foot), Z front to back (positive at the back). Plotting X against Y gives the frontal loop, X against Z the horizontal loop, Y against Z the sagittal loop. At each instant the tip of the heart vector traces a path, so one QRS complex becomes one closed QRS loop. The P loop is small, the QRS loop large, the T loop intermediate. Cardiologists read the loop's rotation direction, area and the magnitude and angle of the maximum vector.

spec.aria: ECG paper grid with a 10 millimetre calibration bar and two heartbeats whose R peaks are 18 millimetres apart, the QRS complex 2 millimetres wide, with boxes converting to 0.72 seconds, 83.3 beats per minute and 0.08 seconds.

examples.question: An ECG is recorded at a paper speed of 25 mm/s with calibration 1 mV = 10 mm. On the strip, the RR interval measures 18 mm and the QRS complex is 2.0 mm wide along the time axis. Find the RR interval in seconds, the heart rate in beats per minute, and the QRS duration in seconds and in milliseconds.
steps: Time scale: 1 mm of paper = 1/25 s = 0.04 s.
Heart rate = 60 / 0.72 s = 83.3 beats per minute.
examples.answer: RR interval 0.72 s, heart rate 83.3 bpm, QRS duration 0.08 s or 80 ms.
examples.check:
speed = 25.0
rr_mm = 18.0
qrs_mm = 2.0
rr = rr_mm / speed
hr = 60 / rr
qrs = qrs_mm / speed
print(round(rr, 2))
print(round(hr, 1))
print(round(qrs, 2))
print(round(qrs * 1000, 1))

traps: Paper speed sets time and calibration sets voltage. A trace can look normal and still be wrong if the 1 mV bar is not 10 mm tall.
Einthoven's law is II = I + III. Reversing signs, or writing I = II + III, is the most common slip.
At 25 mm/s one small square is 0.04 s. Students often use 0.02 s, the value at 50 mm/s, and halve every duration.
aVR is normally negative for P, QRS and T because the heart vector points away from the right arm. A positive aVR is a finding, not a normal variant.
VCG is not a different signal. It uses orthogonal Frank leads X, Y and Z on the same electrical activity, so a normal ECG and a normal VCG must agree.

quiz.q: Define an ECG lead and name the three standard bipolar limb leads.
quiz.a: A lead is a fixed pair of electrodes with a defined polarity that gives one view of the heart's electrical activity. The bipolar limb leads are I (LA − RA), II (LL − RA) and III (LL − LA).

quiz.q: State Einthoven's law and the standard calibration and paper speed of an ECG recorder.
quiz.a: II = I + III. Calibration is 1 mV = 10 mm (10 mm/mV) and standard paper speed is 25 mm/s.

quiz.q: Why does the ECG bio-amplifier need a very high common-mode rejection ratio?
quiz.a: The wanted signal is about 1 mV, while 50 Hz mains pickup appears equally on both input electrodes as a common-mode voltage that is often hundreds of millivolts. A CMRR above 100 dB rejects that shared voltage and leaves the small difference readable.

quiz.q: Why must the paper speed be known before any duration is measured on an ECG strip?
quiz.a: The horizontal axis is distance, not time. Duration equals measured length divided by paper speed, so 1 mm means 0.04 s at 25 mm/s but 0.02 s at 50 mm/s. Without the speed, a width in mm cannot be converted to seconds.

quiz.q: A strip recorded at 50 mm/s shows an RR interval of 40 mm and a QRS width of 5 mm. Find the heart rate and the QRS duration.
quiz.a: 1 mm = 1/50 s = 0.02 s. RR = 40 × 0.02 = 0.8 s. Heart rate = 60 / 0.8 = 75 bpm. QRS = 5 × 0.02 = 0.10 s = 100 ms, within the normal 0.06–0.10 s range.

quiz.q: The 1 mV calibration pulse on a recorder produces a bar 7 mm tall instead of 10 mm. By what percentage is every voltage reading wrong, and what is the actual sensitivity?
quiz.a: Actual sensitivity = 7 mm/mV instead of 10 mm/mV. Error = (10 − 7)/10 × 100 = 30% too low. A wave measured as 1.4 mm is really 1.4/7 = 0.2 mV, not 0.14 mV.

quiz.q: A 12-lead ECG at 25 mm/s shows a QRS 3 mm wide with no visible P wave before it. What does this suggest, and what should be checked first?
quiz.a: 3 mm at 25 mm/s is 0.12 s, at the borderline and conventionally called wide, and the missing P wave points to a ventricular rhythm or atrial fibrillation with aberrant conduction. Before diagnosing, check that the paper speed is really 25 mm/s and that the calibration bar is 10 mm, then check limb electrode placement, because a wrong speed or a swapped arm lead can imitate both findings.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern ECG machines sample at 500 Hz to 1 kHz per channel and store raw data, so paper speed becomes a display setting, and software measures PR, QRS and QT against age- and sex-specific limits. Vectorcardiography returns inside these programs: X, Y and Z are computed from the 12 leads and the QRS loop is shown in 3D. Search terms: Frank lead system, spatial QRS-T angle, patch ECG.
